China-US CN.name: China-US CN
China-US CN.owners: AT&T, China Telecom, Chunghwa Telecom, HKT, KDD, KT, MCI, NTT, SBC, SingTel, Sprint, Telekom Malaysia, Teleglobe, Telstra
China-US CN.description: Commissioned in 2000, China-US Cable Network was a 30,000 km transpacific fiber-optic ring connecting the United States mainland and Guam with China, Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea. Built by an international consortium of over 40 carriers with a design capacity of 80 Gbps across four fiber pairs, it served as the dominant digital bridge between China and the US during the early 2000s internet explosion. China-US CN was decommissioned in December 2016 after 16 years of service, retired as modern systems like Trans-Pacific Express (TPE) and NCP assumed transpacific workloads.

landingPoints.name: San Luis Obispo, CA, United States

Japan-US CN.name: Japan-US CN
Japan-US CN.owners: KDD, NTT, Japan Telecom, AT&T, Level 3, MCI WorldCom, Qwest, SBC, Sprint, Teleglobe, BT, Cable & Wireless, SingTel, Telstra
Japan-US CN.description: Commissioned in 2001, Japan-US Cable Network was a 20,800 km self-healing fiber-optic ring linking Japan and the United States across six landing stations, built across four fiber pairs by supplier KDD-SCS with an initial design capacity of 640 Gbps. It was repeatedly upgraded with 10 Gbps, 40 Gbps, and 100 Gbps coherent DWDM technologies, multiplying its capacity to over 10 Tbps. Japan-US CN was officially decommissioned in 2023 after 22 years of service, retired due to aging repeaters and the commissioning of modern high-fiber-count systems like JUPITER and FASTER.

TAT-14.name: TAT-14
TAT-14.owners: AT&T, BT, C&W, Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, KPN, MCII, PGE, Sprint, Swisscom and Telia
TAT-14.description: Commissioned in 2001, TAT-14 was a 15,428 km transatlantic submarine cable system linking the United States with the UK, France, the Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark in a protected SDH ring. Built by an 11-carrier consortium and supplier KDD Submarine Cable Systems for $1.2 billion, it initially operated at 1.87 Tbps and was later upgraded with 40 Gbps DWDM to 9.38 Tbps. TAT-14 was officially decommissioned in December 2020 after nearly two decades of operation, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and the availability of modern petabit-class cables, after which its North Atlantic shore ends and deep-sea sections were recovered for recycling.

TAT-8.name: TAT-8
TAT-8.description: Commissioned in December 1988, TAT-8 was the world's first transatlantic submarine fiber-optic cable, stretching 6,144 km between Tuckerton, New Jersey, Widemouth Bay, UK, and Penmarch, France, via an undersea branching unit off the continental shelf. Built by AT&T, France Telecom, and British Telecom with 1.3-micron lasers and two active fiber pairs operating at 280 Mbps (SL system), it provided 40,000 simultaneous voice channels—ten times more than all previous transatlantic copper cables combined. TAT-8 was decommissioned in 2002 after 14 years of historic service, retired as modern DWDM fiber networks offered hundreds of times more capacity.

TAT-9.name: TAT-9
TAT-9.description: Commissioned in 1992, TAT-9 was a 9,000 km transatlantic fiber-optic system linking the United States and Canada with the UK, France, and Spain through multiple undersea branching units. Operating at 560 Mbps per fiber pair, it incorporated early digital branching technology for dynamic traffic routing. TAT-9 was decommissioned in 2004 after 12 years of service, retired as multi-wavelength DWDM networks drastically reduced transoceanic bandwidth costs.

TPC-3.name: TPC-3
TPC-3.description: Commissioned in 1989, TPC-3 was the first digital fiber-optic cable across the Pacific, linking Point Arena, California, to Makaha, Hawaii, Guam, and Chikura, Japan, over 13,300 km. Built by AT&T and KDD operating at 280 Mbps per fiber pair (SL100/FS-400M systems), it ushered in the digital optical era across the Pacific. TPC-3 was decommissioned in 2003 after 14 years of service, retired as modern DWDM multi-gigabit fiber systems made 280 Mbps trunking obsolete.

PTAT-1.name: PTAT-1
PTAT-1.owners: Tel-Optik (PSI, Inc.), Cable & Wireless, later Sprint
PTAT-1.description: Commissioned in 1989, PTAT-1 (Private Transatlantic Telecommunications System 1) was the world's first privately financed, non-consortium transatlantic fiber-optic cable, spanning 7,000 km between Manasquan, New Jersey, and Bude, England, with a spur to Bermuda. Financed by Cable & Wireless and Tel-Optik, it operated at 420 Mbps across three fiber pairs, pioneering commercial open-market competition against traditional national telecom carrier cartels. PTAT-1 was decommissioned in 2004 after 15 years of groundbreaking service.

1858 Cable.name: 1858 Cable
1858 Cable.owners: Atlantic Telegraph Company, U.S. and British Governments
1858 Cable.description: Laid in 1858 by the Atlantic Telegraph Company with backing from the British and American governments, the 1858 Cable was the first transatlantic telegraph cable in history, stretching 3,108 km from Valentia Island, Ireland, to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland. Transported and laid by the naval steamships HMS Agamemnon and USS Niagara, the system transmitted Queen Victoria's historic message to President James Buchanan, proving transoceanic electrical communications were feasible. However, its gutta-percha insulation deteriorated rapidly under excessive high voltage applied by electrician E.O. Whitehouse, resulting in total electrical failure and retirement after only three weeks of operation in 1858.

1866 Cable.name: 1866 Cable
1866 Cable.description: Completed in July 1866, the 1866 Cable was the first permanently successful transatlantic telegraph system, spanning 3,500 km between Valentia Island, Ireland, and Heart's Content, Newfoundland. Laid by Isambard Kingdom Brunel's massive iron steamship SS Great Eastern, the cable featured heavily armored seven-strand copper wire insulated with four layers of Chatterton's compound and gutta-percha. The enterprise established dependable intercontinental commerce and news transmission for the Anglo-American Telegraph Company, operating for decades until telegraph obsolescence led to its decommissioning in 1965.

UK-Australia (1870).name: UK-Australia (1870)
UK-Australia (1870).owners: British-Australian Telegraph Company, Eastern Telegraph Company
UK-Australia (1870).description: Commissioned in 1872 by the British-Australian Telegraph Company, this landmark 3,100 km submarine cable connected Banyuwangi, Java, to Darwin, Australia, integrating Australia into the global telegraph network via the overland telegraph line to Adelaide. It reduced communication times between Britain and Australia from three months by steamship to mere hours, transforming imperial administration and global commodities trade. The historic system operated for nearly a century before being decommissioned in 1970 with the emergence of high-capacity coaxial and satellite links.

French Atlantic (1898).name: French Atlantic (1898)
French Atlantic (1898).description: Known colloquially as 'Le Direct', this 5,878 km French transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in 1898 by the Compagnie Française des Câbles Télégraphiques between Brest, France, and Cape Cod (Orleans), Massachusetts. It was celebrated as the longest single non-stop telegraph span in the world without an intermediate relay station, delivering immediate communications between Paris and New York. The cable operated through two world wars before being retired in 1959 as transatlantic coaxial telephone systems (TAT-1) made long-distance telegraphy obsolete.

All Red Line (1902).name: All Red Line (1902)
All Red Line (1902).owners: Pacific Cable Board (governments of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, etc.)
All Red Line (1902).description: Completed in 1902 by the Pacific Cable Board, the All Red Line was a strategic British imperial telegraph network spanning 14,000 km across the Pacific from Bamfield, British Columbia, to Fanning Island, Fiji, Norfolk Island, New Zealand, and Australia. Designed to create a secure globe-spanning communication link passing entirely through British territory without foreign intercept points, it completed the first circumnavigation of the globe by telegraph. The system was decommissioned in 1970 when modern coaxial systems like COMPAC assumed its telecommunications workload.

First Transpacific (1903).name: First Transpacific (1903)
First Transpacific (1903).owners: Commercial Pacific Cable Company (Commercial Cable Co., Great Northern Telegraph Co., Eastern Telegraph Co.)
First Transpacific (1903).description: Completed on July 4, 1903, by the Commercial Pacific Cable Company, this 12,900 km telegraph network was the first submarine cable across the central Pacific, linking San Francisco to Honolulu, Midway Island, Guam, and Manila, Philippines. The inaugural message was sent by President Theodore Roosevelt circling the globe in 12 minutes, establishing direct American communications to Hawaii and newly acquired Pacific territories. The line operated through World War II until its decommissioning in 1951 due to deep-sea fault damage and the rise of transpacific radio-telephone channels.

Key West-Havana Cable.name: Key West-Havana Cable
Key West-Havana Cable.owners: Cuban American Telephone & Telegraph Company (AT&T, ITT)
Key West-Havana Cable.description: Installed in 1921 by AT&T and the Cuban American Telephone and Telegraph Company, the Key West-Havana system comprised three submarine coaxial cables spanning 185 km across the Straits of Florida. It was a pioneering engineering milestone that achieved the world's first commercial deep-water carrier telephone transmission using vacuum tube amplification and permalloy tape loading. The system provided crystal-clear voice links between Cuba and the North American telephone network until its decommissioning in 1988 after microwave and satellite links took over.

TAT-1.name: TAT-1
TAT-1.owners: UK's GPO, AT&T, Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation
TAT-1.description: Commissioned on September 25, 1956, TAT-1 was the world's first transatlantic submarine telephone cable system, stretching 3,600 km between Gallanach Bay near Oban, Scotland, and Clarenville, Newfoundland. Jointly built by AT&T, the British General Post Office, and Teleglobe Canada, TAT-1 utilized twin coaxial cables equipped with 51 flexible underwater vacuum-tube repeaters engineered by Bell Labs, providing 36 simultaneous high-clarity telephone circuits. The system carried the Washington-Moscow 'hotline' during the Cold War before being retired in 1978 after 22 years of continuous operation, decommissioned as larger coaxial systems (TAT-6) and satellite links superseded its capacity.

TAT-2.name: TAT-2
TAT-2.owners: AT&T, and national operators of Germany and France
TAT-2.description: Entering service in 1959, TAT-2 was a transatlantic coaxial telephone cable connecting Penmarch, France, with Clarenville, Newfoundland, spanning 4,200 km. Modeled after the groundbreaking TAT-1 architecture, it was constructed by AT&T, the French PTT, and the German Deutsche Bundespost to establish direct high-grade voice channels between continental Europe and North America. TAT-2 was retired in 1982 after 23 years of operation, decommissioned as higher-capacity transatlantic coaxial systems and satellite links eclipsed its modest 48 voice channels.

TAT-3.name: TAT-3
TAT-3.description: Commissioned in 1963, TAT-3 was a 6,500 km transatlantic coaxial telephone cable connecting Tuckerton, New Jersey, directly to Widemouth Bay, England, without an intermediate Canadian relay point. It was the first transatlantic cable to utilize AT&T's new single-cable SD system with rigid bidirectional repeaters, carrying 138 simultaneous voice circuits. TAT-3 was decommissioned in 1986 after 23 years of service, having reached the end of its design life as modern fiber-optic technology loomed.

TAT-4.name: TAT-4
TAT-4.description: Commissioned in 1965, TAT-4 was a transatlantic coaxial telephone cable spanning 5,880 km between Tuckerton, New Jersey, and Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez, France. Built with AT&T's SD coaxial technology and rigid repeaters, it provided 138 high-grade voice channels directly linking the United States and France. The system operated reliably until its decommissioning in 1987, retired after 22 years of service in anticipation of the world's first transatlantic fiber-optic cable (TAT-8).

TAT-5.name: TAT-5
TAT-5.description: Commissioned in 1970, TAT-5 was a 6,100 km southern transatlantic coaxial cable connecting Green Hill, Rhode Island, to Conil de la Frontera, Spain. Deploying AT&T's SF coaxial system, it provided 720 simultaneous voice circuits, connecting the United States to Mediterranean networks and the Iberian peninsula. TAT-5 was decommissioned in 1993 after 23 years of service, retired due to high maintenance costs and the complete shift of transatlantic telecommunications to high-speed fiber-optic rings.

TAT-6.name: TAT-6
TAT-6.description: Entering service in 1976, TAT-6 was a high-capacity transatlantic coaxial cable spanning 6,400 km between Green Hill, Rhode Island, and Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez, France. Featuring the SG-design coaxial cable with a 1.7-inch diameter core, it carried 4,000 voice channels, an immense jump over previous generations. TAT-6 was retired in 1994 after 18 years of service, decommissioned as digital fiber-optic cables (TAT-8 through TAT-11) rendered analog coaxial transmission obsolete.

TAT-7.name: TAT-7
TAT-7.description: Commissioned in 1983, TAT-7 was the final transatlantic coaxial copper cable ever installed, spanning 6,160 km from Tuckerton, New Jersey, to Land's End, United Kingdom. With an SG coaxial capacity of 4,200 voice circuits, it served as the analog telecommunications workhorse of the early 1980s. TAT-7 was decommissioned in 1994 after only 11 years of service, retired prematurely because newly deployed transatlantic fiber-optic networks provided vastly superior digital capacity and lower per-circuit operational costs.

ANZCAN.name: ANZCAN
ANZCAN.owners: Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Fiji, Norfolk Island
ANZCAN.description: Commissioned in 1984, the ANZCAN cable was a 15,100 km transpacific coaxial cable linking Vancouver, Canada, with Hawaii, Fiji, Norfolk Island, New Zealand, and Sydney, Australia. Providing 1,380 telephone channels, it was the largest single telecommunications project in the Southern Hemisphere at the time. ANZCAN operated until 2001, when it was decommissioned after 17 years as transpacific fiber systems (Southern Cross) took over traffic.

COMPAC.name: COMPAC
COMPAC.owners: Commonwealth countries (Canada, New Zealand, Australia, UK)
COMPAC.description: Commissioned in 1963, the Commonwealth Pacific Cable (COMPAC) was a massive 15,100 km coaxial telephone network linking Vancouver, Canada, to Honolulu, Fiji, New Zealand, and Sydney, Australia. Part of the British Commonwealth round-the-world cable scheme, it utilized lightweight unarmored deep-sea coaxial cable with British repeaters to deliver 80 high-clarity voice circuits across the Pacific. COMPAC operated for 21 years until its retirement in 1984, decommissioned when the higher-capacity ANZCAN coaxial cable took over.

TPC-1.name: TPC-1
TPC-1.owners: AT&T, Hawaiian Telephone Company (HTC), Kokusai Denshin Denwa (KDD)
TPC-1.description: Commissioned in 1964, Transpacific-1 (TPC-1) was the first submarine telephone cable across the Pacific, spanning 9,700 km from Makaha, Hawaii, to Guam and Ninomiya, Japan. Jointly constructed by AT&T and KDD, it carried 128 voice circuits using SD coaxial technology and rigid repeaters, dramatically transforming transpacific commerce and diplomacy. TPC-1 was decommissioned in 1990 after 26 years of service, retired as transpacific fiber optics (TPC-3) took over international traffic.

TPC-2.name: TPC-2
TPC-2.description: Entering service in 1976, Transpacific-2 (TPC-2) was a 10,700 km coaxial cable connecting Oahu, Hawaii, with Guam, Taiwan, and Okinawa, Japan. Delivering 845 voice circuits via AT&T's SF coaxial system, it reinforced transpacific communications during East Asia's economic boom. TPC-2 was decommissioned in 1994 after 18 years of service, retired when optical fiber networks (TPC-4 and TPC-5CN) made analog coaxial cables economically unviable.

TPC-5CN.name: TPC-5CN
TPC-5CN.capacity: 5 Gbps per fiber pair (10 Gbps total)
TPC-5CN.description: Commissioned in 1996, the TPC-5 Cable Network was a 25,000 km self-healing fiber-optic ring connecting the United States mainland, Hawaii, Guam, and Japan across the Pacific. It was the first transpacific system to use optical amplifiers (EDFA) and 5 Gbps line rates in a protected ring configuration. TPC-5CN was decommissioned in 2019 after 23 years of operation, retired near the end of its 25-year design life as modern coherent systems like FASTER, JUPITER, and NCP took over transpacific routes.

TAT-10.name: TAT-10
TAT-10.owners: AT&T, Deutsche Bundespost Telekom, PTT Telecom Netherlands
TAT-10.description: Commissioned in 1992, TAT-10 was an 8,400 km transatlantic fiber-optic cable linking Green Hill, Rhode Island, with Norden, Germany, and the Netherlands. Designed with 560 Mbps transmission per fiber pair, it offered direct high-speed digital pathways into northern Europe. TAT-10 was decommissioned in 2003 after 11 years of service following commercial consolidation and the deployment of terabit-scale DWDM rings.

landingPoints.name: Green Hill, Rhode Island, United States

TAT-11.name: TAT-11
TAT-11.description: Commissioned in 1993, TAT-11 was a 7,120 km transatlantic fiber-optic cable connecting Manasquan, New Jersey, with St. Valery, France, and the UK. Operating at 560 Mbps, it expanded transoceanic digital connectivity prior to the commercial internet boom. TAT-11 was retired in 2003 after a decade of operation, decommissioned as modern DWDM networks made older PDH/SDH transmission economically unviable.

TAT-12-13.name: TAT-12-13
TAT-12-13.description: Commissioned in 1996, the TAT-12/13 cable network was a 12,400 km transatlantic fiber-optic ring connecting the US, UK, and France using erbium-doped optical amplifiers (EDFA). Operating initially at 5 Gbps and later upgraded with DWDM to 10 Gbps per pair, it was among the earliest optical-amplifier rings across the Atlantic. TAT-12/13 was decommissioned in 2008 after 12 years of service, retired as next-generation terabit cables (Apollo, TAT-14) superseded its architecture.

landingPoints.name: Green Hill, Rhode Island, United States

APC.name: APC
APC.owners: KDD, Chunghwa Telecom, Hong Kong Telecom, Telekom Malaysia, SingTel, AT&T
APC.description: Commissioned in 1993, APC is a 7,516 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking Japan, Taiwan, China, and other regional landing points, developed by a consortium led by KDD and Chunghwa Telecom. Engineered with a 2-fiber-pair architecture and a design capacity of 5 Gbps supplied by Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. After approximately 12 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2005 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

APCN.name: APCN
APCN.owners: KDDI, Korea Telecom, Chunghwa Telecom, Cable & Wireless, PLDT, SingTel, Telekom Indonesia, CAT Thailand, Telstra
APCN.description: Commissioned in 1997, APCN is a 12,083 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and other regional landing points, developed by a consortium led by KDDI and Korea Telecom. Engineered with a 2-fiber-pair architecture and a design capacity of 5 Gbps supplied by Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. After approximately 19 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2016 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

Columbus-III.name: Columbus-III
Columbus-III.owners: AT&T, Verizon, Telxius, Portugal Telecom, Tata Communications, Telecom Italia Sparkle, Telkom South Africa, Embratel
Columbus-III.description: Commissioned in 1999, Columbus-III is a 9,900 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking United States, Portugal, Spain, and other regional landing points, developed by a consortium led by AT&T and Verizon. Engineered with a 2-fiber-pair architecture and a design capacity of 20 Gbps, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system was decommissioned in 2020 following the end of its planned commercial design life as newer high-density fiber systems superseded its transmission capabilities.

Gemini.name: Gemini
Gemini.description: Commissioned in 1998, Gemini is a 11,500 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking United States, Bermuda, and United Kingdom, jointly owned by Cable & Wireless and MCI WorldCom. Engineered with a 4-fiber-pair architecture and a design capacity of 10 Gbps and utilizing dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) supplied by SubCom, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system was decommissioned in 2003 following the end of its planned commercial design life as newer high-density fiber systems superseded its transmission capabilities.

PacRimEast.name: PacRimEast
PacRimEast.owners: Telecom New Zealand, AT&T, Telstra, KDD
PacRimEast.description: Commissioned in 1993, PacRimEast is a 7,700 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting New Zealand and United States, developed by a consortium led by Telecom New Zealand and AT&T. The cable was constructed to deliver dependable high-throughput telecommunications and bolster network resilience along this key corridor. After approximately 16 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2009 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

PacRimWest.name: PacRimWest
PacRimWest.owners: Telstra, AT&T, KDD, Telecom New Zealand
PacRimWest.description: Commissioned in 1995, PacRimWest is a 7,062 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Australia and United States, developed by a consortium led by Telstra and AT&T. Engineered with a 2-fiber-pair architecture supplied by Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. RJK.capacity: 560 Mbps per fiber pair (1.12 Gbps total)
RJK.description: Commissioned in 1995, RJK is a 1,762 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking Russia, Japan, and South Korea, developed by a consortium led by Rostelecom and KDDI. Engineered with a 2-fiber-pair architecture, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. SAT-2.name: SAT-2
SAT-2.owners: Telkom South Africa, Marconi, France Telecom, BT
SAT-2.description: Commissioned in 1993, SAT-2 was a 9,500 km submarine fiber-optic system connecting Melkbosstrand, South Africa, to Sesimbra, Portugal, via Madeira. Operating with 560 Mbps optical transmission, it provided South Africa's primary digital link to Europe during its reintegration into global telecommunications. SAT-2 was retired in 2013 after 20 years of service, decommissioned as the high-capacity SAT-3/WACS systems rendered its legacy bitrates obsolete.

SEA-ME-WE 3.name: SEA-ME-WE 3
SEA-ME-WE 3.owners: SMW3 Consortium (92 telecom operators including Orange, Singtel, Telecom Italia Sparkle, Telekom Malaysia, BT, Deutsche Telekom, KDDI, KT, China Telecom, Chunghwa Telecom, Telstra)
SEA-ME-WE 3.description: Commissioned in 1999, SEA-ME-WE 3 was for years the longest submarine cable system in the world, stretching over 39,000 km across 33 countries and four continents from Western Europe through the Mediterranean, Red Sea, Indian Ocean, and Southeast Asia to Australia and East Asia. Built by an international consortium with 39 landing points, it utilized two fiber pairs with DWDM transmission that underwent multiple capacity upgrades to over 4.6 Tbps. SEA-ME-WE 3 was decommissioned in 2024 after 25 years of service, reaching the end of its 25-year design lifespan as modern systems like SEA-ME-WE 6, PEACE, and 2Africa superseded its network.

landingPoints.name: Deep Water Bay, Hong Kong, China

TPC-4.name: TPC-4
TPC-4.description: Commissioned in 1992, TPC-4 was an 11,500 km transpacific fiber-optic cable connecting Point Arena, California, directly with Port Alberni, Canada, and Chikura, Japan. Designed with 560 Mbps optical transmission, it provided direct non-stop optical paths bypassing Hawaii. TPC-4 was decommissioned in 2006 after 14 years of operation, retired as dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) cables like Japan-US and PC-1 offered hundreds of times more capacity.

SEA-ME-WE 1.name: SEA-ME-WE 1
SEA-ME-WE 1.owners: Consortium of 22 international carriers (France Telecom, Telecom Italia, OTE, Telecom Egypt, STC, Djibouti Telecom, VSNL, Sri Lanka Telecom, Singtel)
SEA-ME-WE 1.description: Commissioned in 1986, South East Asia-Middle East-Western Europe 1 (SEA-ME-WE 1) was a 13,500 km undersea coaxial cable system connecting France to Singapore via Egypt, Saudi Arabia, India, and Sri Lanka. Built by an international consortium of 22 carriers, it was the first submarine cable linking Western Europe and Southeast Asia along the historic Mediterranean-Red Sea-Indian Ocean corridor. It was decommissioned in 1996 after 10 years of service, replaced by the fiber-optic SEA-ME-WE 2 system.

SEA-ME-WE 2.name: SEA-ME-WE 2
SEA-ME-WE 2.owners: Consortium of 60 international carriers (France Telecom, Telecom Italia, STC, Singtel, VSNL, Telkom Indonesia)
SEA-ME-WE 2.description: Commissioned in 1994, SEA-ME-WE 2 was an 18,750 km undersea fiber-optic cable linking 13 countries from Marseille, France, to Singapore via the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. Operating with two fiber pairs at 560 Mbps, it was the first transcontinental fiber-optic cable connecting Europe, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. SEA-ME-WE 2 was decommissioned in 2008 after 14 years of operation, retired as the multi-gigabit SEA-ME-WE 3 and SEA-ME-WE 4 systems took over traffic.

Atlantis-2.name: Atlantis-2
Atlantis-2.owners: Consortium of 25 carriers (Embratel, Telecom Italia, Telefonica, Portugal Telecom, Sonatel, Cabo Verde Telecom)
Atlantis-2.description: Commissioned in 2000, Atlantis-2 is a 12,000 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking Portugal, Spain, Senegal, and other regional landing points, developed by a consortium led by Consortium of 25 carriers (Embratel and Telecom Italia. Engineered with operating with dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. After approximately 21 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2021 following the end of its planned commercial design life as newer high-density fiber systems superseded its transmission capabilities.

CANTAT-1.name: CANTAT-1
CANTAT-1.owners: UK General Post Office, Teleglobe Canada, Cable & Wireless
CANTAT-1.description: Commissioned in 1961, CANTAT-1 was a 3,800 km transatlantic coaxial telephone cable connecting Oban, Scotland, to Corner Brook, Newfoundland. Built for Teleglobe Canada and the British Post Office, it was the first transatlantic cable to deploy lightweight, non-twisting deep-sea coaxial cable, providing 60 high-quality telephone channels. CANTAT-1 was decommissioned in 1986 after 25 years of service, having fulfilled its design lifespan as satellite and digital systems expanded.

CANTAT-2.name: CANTAT-2
CANTAT-2.description: Entering service in 1974, CANTAT-2 was a 5,200 km transatlantic coaxial cable linking Bude, England, to Beaver Harbour, Nova Scotia. Built with high-capacity 1.47-inch coaxial cable, it delivered 1,840 telephone circuits across the North Atlantic for the British Post Office and Teleglobe Canada. CANTAT-2 was decommissioned in 1994 after 20 years of operation, retired following the widespread deployment of transoceanic fiber-optic systems.

HAW-1.name: HAW-1
HAW-1.description: Commissioned in 1957, HAW-1 was the first undersea telephone cable linking the United States mainland (Point Arena, California) to Hanauma Bay, Oahu, Hawaii, over 4,400 km. Built by AT&T and the Hawaiian Telephone Company using twin SB coaxial cables, it provided 36 voice channels that replaced erratic high-frequency radio. HAW-1 was decommissioned in 1989 after 32 years of continuous operation, retired as the first transpacific fiber-optic cable (HAW-4/TPC-3) entered service.

HAW-2.name: HAW-2
HAW-2.description: Commissioned in 1964, HAW-2 was a 4,400 km coaxial cable connecting San Luis Obispo, California, to Makaha, Hawaii. Built with AT&T's SD coaxial system, it provided 128 voice channels connecting mainland networks with the western Pacific via TPC-1. HAW-2 was decommissioned in 1989 after 25 years of service, retired in favor of transpacific digital fiber networks.

It served as a primary commercial telecommunications link to Hawaii during the 1970s and 1980s before being decommissioned in 1989 as digital fiber optics transformed transpacific communications.

Installed in conjunction with TPC-3, it introduced commercial transpacific digital fiber connectivity. HAW-4 was decommissioned in 2002 after 13 years of service, retired when modern DWDM cables provided gigabit and terabit bandwidth.

It was the first undersea telephone cable linking southern Africa directly with Europe, providing 360 high-grade voice channels for the South African Post Office. SAT-1 was decommissioned in 1993 after 24 years of service, succeeded by the digital fiber-optic SAT-2 and SAT-3 cables.

French Atlantic (1869).name: French Atlantic (1869)
French Atlantic (1869).description: Commissioned in 1869 by the Société du Câble Transatlantique Français, the French Atlantic telegraph cable spanned 5,800 km from Brest, France, to Duxbury, Massachusetts, via Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. Laid by the SS Great Eastern, it was the first transatlantic telegraph line directly serving France and the longest single telegraph cable of its era. The system broke the Anglo-American Telegraph Company's transatlantic monopoly before being decommissioned in 1894 due to severe deep-sea conductor faults and newer parallel routes.

Direct United States Cable (1874).name: Direct United States Cable (1874)
Direct United States Cable (1874).owners: Direct United States Cable Company (Siemens Brothers)
Direct United States Cable (1874).description: Commissioned in 1874, the Direct United States Cable was built by Siemens Brothers to create an independent telegraph route linking Ballinskelligs Bay, Ireland, to Rye Beach, New Hampshire, via Halifax, Nova Scotia. Engineered by William Siemens and laid by the newly built cable ship Faraday, it bypassed Newfoundland to avoid the Anglo-American cartel's exclusive landing concessions. The system operated reliably for half a century until its decommissioning in 1923 as newer multi-channel telegraph lines replaced early single-wire links.

APNG-2.name: APNG-2
APNG-2.description: Commissioned in 2006, APNG-2 is a 1,800 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Australia and Papua New Guinea, jointly owned by Telstra and PNG DataCo. Engineered with a 2-fiber-pair architecture and operating with dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) supplied by Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system was decommissioned in 2019 following the end of its planned commercial design life as newer high-density fiber systems superseded its transmission capabilities.

Guam-Philippines.name: Guam-Philippines
Guam-Philippines.description: Commissioned in 1989, Guam-Philippines is a 2,400 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Guam and Philippines, jointly owned by AT&T and PLDT. Engineered with a design capacity of 40 Gbps, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. After approximately 14 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2003 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

Italy-Greece 1.name: Italy-Greece 1
Italy-Greece 1.description: Commissioned in 1995, Italy-Greece 1 is a 320 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Italy and Greece, jointly owned by Telecom Italia Sparkle and OTE. Engineered with a design capacity of 400 Gbps, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. After approximately 20 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2015 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

Qatar-UAE.name: Qatar-UAE
Qatar-UAE.description: Commissioned in 1996, Qatar-UAE is a 200 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Qatar and United Arab Emirates, jointly owned by Ooredoo and Etisalat. The cable was constructed to deliver dependable high-throughput telecommunications and bolster network resilience along this key corridor. After approximately 20 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2016 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

MIC-3.name: MIC-3
MIC-3.description: Commissioned in 1989, MIC-3 is a 2,300 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Italy and Israel, jointly owned by Bezeq and Telecom Italia. Engineered with a 32-fiber-pair architecture supplied by HMN Technologies (formerly Huawei Marine), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. After approximately 20 years of commercial operation, the system was retired in 2009 after reaching the end of its operational lifespan, retired due to high wet-plant maintenance costs and capacity obsolescence compared to modern coherent DWDM networks.

Commercial Cable 1884.name: Commercial Cable 1884
Commercial Cable 1884.description: Financed by copper magnate John William Mackay and publisher James Gordon Bennett Jr. in 1884, the Commercial Cable Company installed twin transatlantic telegraph cables between Waterville, Ireland, and Canso, Nova Scotia. The 4,500 km system was constructed to break Jay Gould's Western Union monopoly on transatlantic rates, triggering a dramatic drop in transatlantic telegraph fees. Operating with duplex transmission, the system served international news wires and financial markets until it was decommissioned in 1928.

Anglo-American 1873.name: Anglo-American 1873
Anglo-American 1873.description: Laid in 1873 by the Anglo-American Telegraph Company using the SS Great Eastern, this 3,500 km transatlantic telegraph cable linked Valentia Island, Ireland, with Heart's Content, Newfoundland. Designed with heavy iron armor for the shallow continental shelves and robust gutta-percha core insulation, it dramatically increased telegraphic throughput across the North Atlantic to meet burgeoning financial trading demand. The system was decommissioned in 1910 when multiple deep-water breaks and technological advances in multiplexed telegraphy made its repair economically unviable.

German Atlantic 1900.name: German Atlantic 1900
German Atlantic 1900.description: Laid in 1900 by the German Atlantic Telegraph Company (DAT), this 7,920 km cable linked Emden, Germany, to New York via Horta in the Azores, providing the German Empire with direct communications independent of British networks. It was cut and decommissioned in 1914 during World War I by the Royal Navy cable ship CS Telconia to sever German communications, with segments later diverted into Allied service.

Palau Cable 1.name: Palau Cable 1
Palau Cable 1.description: Commissioned in 2017, Palau Cable 1 is a 200 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Palau and Guam, operated by Belau Submarine Cable Corporation (BSCC). Engineered with operating with dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system remains an active link in the global telecommunications grid, supporting regional internet transit and commercial data exchange.

Palau Cable 2.name: Palau Cable 2
Palau Cable 2.description: Commissioned in 2024, Palau Cable 2 is a 150 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Palau and Guam, operated by Belau Submarine Cable Corporation (BSCC). Engineered with a design capacity of 100Gbps and delivering high-capacity coherent optical transmission supplied by NEC, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. It represents modern next-generation subsea infrastructure designed to support cloud computing, mobile data growth, and international internet traffic.

American Samoa Hawaii (ASH).name: American Samoa Hawaii (ASH)
American Samoa Hawaii (ASH).description: Commissioned in 2009, American Samoa Hawaii (ASH) is a 3,922 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting American Samoa and United States, operated by American Samoa Hawaii Cable LLC. Engineered with operating with dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system remains an active link in the global telecommunications grid, supporting regional internet transit and commercial data exchange.

Amber.name: Amber
Amber.description: Commissioned in 2014, Amber is a 260 km submarine fiber-optic cable system connecting Latvia and Sweden, operated by Latvenergo. Engineered with operating with dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM), the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system remains an active link in the global telecommunications grid, supporting regional internet transit and commercial data exchange.

SednaLink.name: SednaLink
SednaLink.description: Commissioned in 2023, SednaLink is a 420 km submarine fiber-optic cable system within Canada, operated by Eeyou Communications Network. Engineered with delivering high-capacity coherent optical transmission, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. It represents modern next-generation subsea infrastructure designed to support cloud computing, mobile data growth, and international internet traffic.

WALL-LI.name: WALL-LI
WALL-LI.description: Commissioned in 2021, WALL-LI is a 80 km submarine fiber-optic cable system within United States, operated by Crosslake Fibre. Engineered with delivering high-capacity coherent optical transmission, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. The system remains an active link in the global telecommunications grid, supporting regional internet transit and commercial data exchange.

BlueMed.name: BlueMed
BlueMed.capacity: 30 Tbps per fiber pair (120 Tbps total, 4 FPs; 25 Tbps/FP initial)
BlueMed.description: Commissioned in 2023, BlueMed is a 1,500 km submarine fiber-optic cable system linking Italy, France, and Greece, operated by Sparkle. Engineered with a 4-fiber-pair architecture and delivering high-capacity coherent optical transmission, the cable was built to meet expanding international digital bandwidth demands and reinforce regional route diversity. It represents modern next-generation subsea infrastructure designed to support cloud computing, mobile data growth, and international internet traffic.
